30 inventorship days in 8 years: 6 reasons why we keep hacking

Article by Kimi George
Published on 23rd Mar 2018 — Read in 4 mins

Share

  • Tweet about it
  • Share this on LinkedIn
  • Share this on Facebook

We have reached our 8th anniversary of Inventorship Days – eight years and 30 events, it’s a pretty big milestone! I therefore thought it’d be a good idea to reflect over the last eight years on the true business value of these events and share some insights into why I think these events are important for not only our business, but other companies considering starting one in their workplace.

Building cross functional trust & relationships

To maintain the success of the event, we need to encourage participation from a diverse range of business functions.  We know complex problems are better solved by a group of people who have different backgrounds, but visitors to REA Group are often surprised when they see that our Inventorship Days encompass more than just our tech community.

Every quarter we see pitches from all across the business including legal, facilities, our customer service team, product, marketing, and sales. You may find yourself on a team with someone in the office that you’ve never met before, or get the chance to be working on a project you know nothing about, but the beauty of our events is seeing a whole lot of people bringing all of their skills to the table.

The best outcome is knowing people leave the three days thinking things like, ‘Wow, Lisa from legal really knows her s**t. The next time I need a legal consult as part of a project I’m working on, I already know and trust Lisa’s work’. When I hear stories like this, I know we’ve succeeded at running a truly successful, cross functional team event.

Practice makes perfect

Inventing things is hard and it doesn’t come easily to most, but by setting a regular time for Inventorship every quarter, our people know there is always another chance to get their idea right, or try something new.  We put great emphasis on sharing knowledge, so our inventors learn from what has been done before them and as a result, we’ve noticed the calibre of our ideas greatly improving over time.

Everyone has something to teach. Everyone has something to learn 

Knot your Nanna’s were a team who came together to knit squares, which were then joined to make blankets and donated to not-for-profit organisation ‘Knit One Give One’.  Some people were experienced knitters, while others came to learn about different knitting styles (including crochet), different knitting machines, and different yarn types.  The team brought together Software Developers, Business Analysts, Delivery Leads, UX, Marketing and Finance functions. Even our Chief Inventor’s wife came in to lend a helping hand.

Now, we know that there is absolutely no tangible correlation between the performance of our business in the market and the number of experienced knitters we have on the payroll, but when  it comes to Inventorship Days, that’s perfectly fine. The beauty of this project is that the process of teaching or learning something, regardless of what that skill is, forces your brain to behave in a different way. You never know where thinking differently, and being inspired by a new skill like knitting, can later lead to.

The act of sharing your particular expertise with your colleagues or, alternatively, reaching out to someone to help you improve your own skills now sits in our DNA.

Developing soft skills

For some people, pitching their idea at the Inventorship Day standup might be the first time they’ve spoken in public.  I take my hat off to everyone who gets up and sells their idea in front of such a large audience, it’s not easy stuff. And then, three days later, teams have to explain what they’ve done or built at our ‘marketplace’, which is often another first-time experience for many.

We no longer have a group of software developers only talking about highly technical concepts while mumbling at their shoes. The marketplace format requires teams to consider their audience first and adjust their pitch accordingly.

These aspects of the Inventorship Days build key soft skills; and they build confidence. It isn’t long before we see the same people delivering talks at external meetups and conferences.

Understanding the product cycle, from idea to delivery

It’s very rare that something seen at the marketplace will ship immediately to market in the same state.  Only one invention out of 100 will appear outside of the REA Group walls as a product innovation, but that’s ok.  We’ve seen different approaches to this at other companies; some will provide delivery teams or idea incubation programs to get their ideas out into market quickly.

While that’s not our approach, every now and then you do get some inventions that capture the eyes of our product managers and get onto the roadmap. Spacely.com.au was an idea that evolved at an Inventorship Day in 2015 and became a brand that launched almost 18 months later in 2017.

Humans love being human

Over the years, our ideas have naturally evolved to embrace more social and community concerns.  In the early days, we assumed people just wanted to play with cool tech so didn’t see this trend coming. As a result, it’s generated some of the most significant benefits and highlighted that our people care – a lot! We care about each other, about their diverse communities, about the environment.
